summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web app that shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real local horizon at 26 lunar landing sites, for any hour of 2027. It answers a mission planner's first questions in seconds: Will the solar panels get light? Can we talk directly to Earth? How long until sunset and Earthset? What changes if we choose another site or date?

At the Moon's south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a small change in location or date can turn days of sunlight into long darkness. Existing tools are powerful but hard for non-specialists. We combined validated NASA data (JPL SPICE ephemeris, LRO LOLA terrain, LROC NAC images) with a clear interface: a 2D sky chart, timelines, heat maps, side-by-side comparison and a 3D Moon you can spin and fly down onto real terrain. A machine-learning crater layer and landing-success estimates help planners pick safer sites and dates. Three modes serve students, educators and mission planners, in English and Turkish.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web application that shows, for any

of 26 lunar landing sites (or custom coordinates) and any hour of 2027,

where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real local horizon. It

answers the four questions mission planners ask first:

- Power: Is the Sun above the terrain? How high? How much energy can a

panel produce (tracking, vertical or horizontal)?

- Communication: Is Earth visible above the terrain plus an antenna

margin, so direct-to-Earth radio is possible?

- Timing: How long until sunset and Earthset? A countdown is always on

screen and turns red under 24 hours.

- Comparison: How do conditions change with a different site or date?

A heat map (site × landing week) and side-by-side comparison answer

this in seconds.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Earth directions come from NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE (DE440, Moon

ME frame), validated against JPL Horizons (0.000° difference). Each

site has a 720-direction horizon profile computed from LRO LOLA

terrain (20 m near the site, 80 m up to 250 km) at the south pole and

SLDEM2015 elsewhere, including lunar curvature, for 0, 2 and 10 m mast

heights. The app computes the visible fraction of the solar disc,

Earth visibility, power, illumination and communication windows,

longest darkness and longest outage. Results match our Python

pipeline exactly; event times agree with SPICE to 0.1 minutes, and

solar illumination correlates 0.96–0.98 with NASA PGDA 69 maps.

A 3D view lets users spin the whole Moon with the real day–night

terminator, click a site and fly down onto its real 10 × 10 km

terrain, where shadows move as time is played. For south-polar sites

[and, where 1 m LROC imagery exists, Apollo and other landing sites –

20 sites in total], the 3D scene can show the real LROC NAC photo,

small craters detected by our own machine-learning model, a crater

hazard map, permanently shadowed areas, and a landing-success

probability for any point that accounts for landing dispersion, slope,

night length versus battery, Earth outages and crater risk. If the

answer is 0%, the app suggests the nearest date when landing there

would succeed.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Tools such as Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons are powerful but

hard for non-specialists to use for quick scenario comparison. Our

contribution is not a new calculation method but a clear interface on

top of validated data. When a launch slips or hardware changes,

planners can see within seconds how a new date or a nearby site

changes power and communication. Three modes serve different users:

Basic (students and the public, with plain-language facts such as

"a day here lasts 29.5 Earth days"), Intermediate (educators) and

Advanced (mission planners, with all engineering parameters and CSV

export). The interface is available in English and Turkish.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data pipeline: Python, NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE (DE440), LRO LOLA and

PGDA terrain, SLDEM2015, LROC NAC images and DTMs.

- Machine learning: YOLOv8s (Ultralytics), trained on an expert crater

catalog (Boazman et al. 2024) and SomBench NAC (NASA–IBM); tested on

unseen polar images (10–20 m craters: 66% recall) and calibrated

against expert labels (mean hazard 0.208 vs 0.198).

- Web app: JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Canvas 2D

(custom charts, no chart library), d3-geo, three.js with

react-three-fiber, Framer Motion. Calculations run in the browser

(Web Workers for heavy steps).

- Hosting: Vercel. Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware.

- AI assistance: the code was written with the help of Claude

(Anthropic). Design decisions, formulas and all validation were done

by the team.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- One continuous journey from the whole Moon down to a landing site's

real terrain, with time playback that moves the Sun, shadows and

Earth together.

- A far-horizon silhouette built from the 250 km terrain profile, so

the 3D scene, the 2D sky chart and the status badges always agree:

when the Sun disappears behind a distant mountain, it does so in

every view.

- A crater card that turns machine-learning output into a decision:

"If you land here: 58% – or try landing on 9 September."

- Concrete Earth-versus-Moon comparisons for younger users (Earth

looks about 4 times larger than the Sun from the Moon).

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: every number comes from a documented calculation and is

tested against reference values; we raised the horizon resolution

to 0.5° after finding that 1° steps changed sunrise and sunset

results at the pole.

- Honesty about uncertainty: coarse estimates, flat-horizon areas and

machine-learning limits are always labeled; the ML confidence score

is shown as "not a probability"; permanently shadowed cells are

marked "unknown", never "safe".

- The south pole's extreme geometry: the Sun skims the horizon, so a

few metres of mast height or a small change in location can change

sunlight from about 50% to over 80%.

- Usability for different skill levels, performance in the browser

(3D loads only when opened) and data credits: NASA/JPL, NASA LRO

LOLA, LROC (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University), NASA's Scientific

Visualization Studio. Not an official NASA product.
